items.title: Running a prototype or pilot
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: A prototype is an early version used to test an idea; a pilot is a small real trial of how it works in practice with real customers. Decide before you start what you want to learn and what result would count as success, for example how many people use it, complete it or pay. Keep it small, set a time limit, and record what happens. Use customers who will tell you the truth, not only friends. At the end, decide with the evidence: go ahead, change it, or stop. A pilot that proves nothing because nobody set a measure only delays the decision.

options.text: A person who flies a plane
A small real trial with real customers

options.text: Friends tend to say what you want to hear

items.title: Making improvements
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Improving a product or service means choosing changes that matter to customers and checking that they worked. Start with evidence: complaints, returns, feedback and what staff see. List possible changes and pick the few with most benefit for the effort. Describe the result you want before you change anything, make the change, and measure the same thing afterwards. Make small changes often rather than large ones rarely, so a mistake is easy to undo. Record what you changed and why. If it did not help, learn from it and stop. Improvement is a habit, not a project.

options.text: With evidence such as feedback, complaints and returns

questions.prompt: Why decide the result you want before you change something?

options.text: So you can tell afterwards whether it worked
A mistake is easy to undo, and you learn faster

questions.prompt: A change did not help. What is the best next step?

options.text: Learn from it and stop or try something else

items.title: Reviewing your range
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: A range review looks at everything you sell and asks which products earn their place. For each, note sales, margin, how much time or stock it ties up, and how it fits what your customers want. Sort into those to keep and push, those to fix (price, quality, position), and those to stop. Be careful with products that sell well but make little profit once costs are counted, and with ones that bring customers in for other purchases. Decide with figures, not habit. Withdraw items properly: sell remaining stock, tell customers and honour what they have bought.

questions.prompt: What does a range review do?

options.text: Checks which products and services earn their place

questions.prompt: What should you note for each product in a range review?

options.text: Sales, margin and the time or stock it ties up

questions.prompt: Why can a product that sells well still be a problem?

options.text: It may make little profit once all costs are counted

questions.prompt: What should you do when you withdraw a product?

options.text: Keep selling the old stock secretly
Sell remaining stock, tell customers and honour what they have bought
